what_happened: Job 20261031-030119-tw3v (add an ordered landing queue with rebase onto latest main to the drain) failed in planning before any code was written. After round 3 of 3 the critic still said the plan needed revising. The critic found the plan well grounded: the functions it names exist and the queue design follows from the code. One major finding remained. The plan's left-behind rule drops a held-back job's landing commit from the local branch when a later job rebases. That commit carries the job's closing records, and Records::load reads job state from that branch. So the rule does the record-dropping drop_landed that the reading had deferred to A6b, and the plan's own decision 1 rejected it. Minor findings: gh/mod.rs is not among the reading's deliverables, though the re-export is needed and disclosed; plan_rebase carries clean unlanded commits, which weakens the NeedsRecheck guarantee the CHANGELOG will state; queue order can differ from stacking order; and the plan is large for one producer run (about 20 tests across two crates). The reading also listed plan_rebase as if it already existed. No acceptance criteria were reported unmet and no checks failed. Nothing was delivered.
cause: Planning does not require a plan to trace what its new rule does to data other parts of the system depend on. Here the left-behind rule removes a commit that carries job records, which the loader reads from that branch. It also does not force the plan to reconcile its own rejected options with its chosen rule. Open questions that the code could settle, and the interactions between the chosen rule and the records design, are left for the critic to find by tracing. Planning has three fixed rounds and keeps no partial plan, so a major finding in the last round loses all planning spend. The sibling job 20261030-013555-f5qm failed the same way on the same core flow. The request bundled a large queue, rebase and records design into one job with no cut line. A size bound that would have forced a split was not applied. The reading also treated new code (plan_rebase) as existing, and nothing checked it against the snapshot.
prevention: Add a required step before the critic in planning for any change to a core flow such as landing. The planner must list every state the change touches, including records and job state read from the landing branch, and every existing caller and mode that reaches the code. For each, it must say how it is affected. Any rule that removes or moves commits must state what records those commits carry. The planner must settle code-answerable questions by reading the code, not leave them open. A plan that reaches the last round with only fixable findings should get one repair round or be kept as a partial plan. Large cores like this should be split at admission into a queue-and-rebase job and a separate records-preserving left-behind job, with a stated cut line.
proposed_request: Add an ordered landing queue with rebase onto latest main to the drain, in two separate jobs. Job 1 delivers only this: when a job passes, it joins a queue in the order it passed. The head job is rebased onto the latest main before it lands. A conflict ends that item without a retry and without stopping the drain. plan_rebase is new code to be written, not an existing function. When a later job rebases, no landing commit may be dropped from the local branch, and every job's closing records must stay readable by Records::load. A job whose commit would conflict is left as it is, with its records kept. Unlanded commits from jobs that are Blocked or NeedsRecheck must not reach main inside another job's pull request. The existing `[parallel] max_concurrency` > 1 path must keep working, and the plan must say how it is affected. Add tests using production plan_rebase and Drain::land, and one CHANGELOG entry that states only what the code guarantees. Do not add drop_landed or any record-removing behavior. Include crates/athena-core/src/gh/mod.rs among the deliverables for the re-export. Defer the carrying of conflicting commits' records without their code to a separate follow-up job.
